context: A companion told him the Sun was not really his father, and he ran to his mother Clymene for the truth. Dante comes just as anxiously to hear the truth about his own future.
In Canto 15 he left his place in the cross of lights and came down to its foot to greet Dante.

quote: no triangle contains two obtuse angles
note: A plain truth of geometry: the three angles of a triangle add up to two right angles, so two of them cannot each be wider than a right angle. The blessed see the future with the same certainty.
A term from philosophy: things that may or may not happen, as against things that must be so. A man's exile is contingent. The sum of a triangle's angles is not.
God, who is outside time. Past, present and future are all present to him at once, and the blessed read the future by looking at him.
Purgatory.

Dark hints of exile, from Farinata in Inferno 10, Brunetto Latini in Inferno 15 and Vanni Fucci in Inferno 24, and from souls in Purgatorio 8 and 11. In Inferno 10 Virgil promised that Beatrice would explain his life's course. In the event she leaves it to his ancestor.
A proverb of the time, known in Latin as well: the blow you see coming hurts less.
The pagan oracles, famous for answers that could be taken two ways. The soul will speak plainly instead.
Christ, so named by John the Baptist in the Gospel of John. The oracles were said to have fallen silent when he came.

The answer to an old puzzle. If God already sees what Dante will do, is Dante still free? Yes: seeing a thing does not cause it, any more than a watcher on the bank moves the ship. The argument goes back to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy.

Son of Theseus, king of Athens. His stepmother Phaedra tried to seduce him, and when he refused she accused him to his father, who drove him out. Dante too will be banished on a false charge, of corruption in office, and Florence will be his cruel stepmother. The story is in Ovid's Metamorphoses.

context: At Easter 1300 he was already working with the Black Guelphs to bring Florence under his control. In 1301 he sent the French prince Charles of Valois to the city as peacemaker. Charles let the Blacks seize power, and Dante was sentenced early in 1302.

note: The papal court at Rome, where Church offices and favors were for sale. The sin is simony, punished in Inferno 19.
Left unnamed. Readers have pointed to the humiliation and death of Boniface in 1303, and to the disasters that struck Florence and the leaders of the Blacks in the years after Dante's exile.
Among the most quoted lines of the poem: the exile's life as a guest in other men's houses, dependent on their favor. Dante's Italian says the bread "tastes of salt".

context: The other exiled Whites, joined by Ghibellines banished earlier. They tried several times to fight their way back into Florence. Dante worked with them at first, then broke away, it seems before their final defeat in 1304.

note: Dante's Italian says their temples will be red, which can mean shame or blood. Most readers see the defeat at La Lastra, outside Florence, in July 1304, where the exiles' attack on the city failed with many dead. Dante was not there.
A famous phrase. Dante ended up belonging to neither side, a Guelph by birth who put his hopes in the emperor, and he makes his isolation a point of honor.

A lord of Verona of the della Scala family, most often identified as Bartolomeo, who ruled until his death in 1304. Dante stayed in Verona early in his exile. The family's name means ladder, and its arms showed a ladder. The eagle above it was the sign of the empire.

quote: what usually comes last will come first
note: The giving will come before the asking. His host will see what Dante needs and offer it unasked.

context: The younger brother of the "great Lombard", and only nine years old in 1300. Dante wrote this when Cangrande was at the height of his power and his own host.

note: Mars, where they are. The planet was thought to make those born under it bold and warlike.

context: He encouraged Henry to come to Italy for the imperial crown, then turned against him once he was there. So the boy's promise will show before about 1312.

note: Dante keeps the rest to himself. Cangrande was alive and still fighting when this was written, so the prophecy of his greatest deeds is left open.

quote: what was prophesied to you before
note: The "grave words" of line 23. What the souls of Hell and Purgatory hinted at darkly has now been said in plain terms.

quote: your life will extend far beyond
note: Dante will outlast his enemies' punishment, in years or, as many read it, in fame. For "extend" his Italian has a verb he made up, s'infutura: his life "futures itself".
The Comedy itself. It names the crimes of living lords and great families. Having lost Florence, Dante could lose every other refuge by telling what he has seen.

quote: my lady's eyes first lifted me
note: The Earthly Paradise at the top of Mount Purgatory. Dante rose from it into the heavens by looking into Beatrice's eyes as she looked at the sun, in Paradiso 1.
Future readers. Dante weighs two fears: lose his welcome now by telling the truth, or lose his name with posterity by hiding it.

quote: let them scratch where it itches
note: A rough proverb, startling this high in Heaven. Dante's Italian names the itch outright: rogna, the mange. Whoever is stung by the poem has earned it.
The poem strikes at popes, kings and great houses, not at small offenders. That takes courage, and so does it honor.

Dante's account of his own method: people are persuaded by examples they recognize. It is not quite the whole truth. Many of the souls he met were obscure, and are remembered today only because he put them in the poem.
